opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question we think about a lot. The way I see it, building an enterprise AI application is like a layered cake. At the top you have the business logic: the specific workflow, the domain knowledge, the data that only the customer really understands. At the bottom you have the raw infrastructure: GPUs, networking, storage, the cloud itself. In the middle there's a thick layer that nobody really wants to own but everybody needs: serving models efficiently, scaling up and down, fine-tuning, monitoring, handling failures when a GPU dies at 3 a.m.

Our rule of thumb is fairly simple. We take on the parts that are hard, repetitive, and not differentiating for the customer. If every company building an AI app has to solve the same problem, and solving it well requires deep systems expertise, that's ours. Making inference fast and cheap, managing heterogeneous compute, making sure a model that runs on a laptop also runs reliably at production scale: that's where our background in frameworks and large-scale infrastructure actually matters.

What we deliberately don't take on is the part where the customer's own knowledge is the moat. We're not going to understand a bank's compliance workflow or a hospital's patient data better than they do. If we tried to build that for them, we'd do a mediocre job and get in their way.

There's also a timing element. The AI stack is changing incredibly fast. Models that were state of the art six months ago are commodities today. So we ask ourselves: will this problem still exist in two or three years, even as the models change? Efficiency, reliability, and cost don't go away. Those are durable problems. A specific prompt-engineering trick might be obsolete next quarter, so we're careful not to over-invest there.

So in short, we want to be the boring, dependable layer that lets enterprises focus on what makes them unique. Cloud computing went through the same thing: in the early days everyone ran their own servers, and eventually people realized that wasn't where the value was. AI is going through that transition now, just much faster.

r001.rationale: The response describes raw infrastructure and the cloud as the bottom layer, but does not say the company avoids building clusters because existing cloud providers are adequate.

r002.rationale: It mentions fine-tuning as a service layer responsibility, but does not connect that to organizing customer data into a clear application pattern or a standardized service.

r003.rationale: It says customers understand their own domain knowledge better, using bank compliance and hospital patient data as examples of decisions the company leaves to them.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question we think about constantly, and honestly the answer has shifted as we've watched the market mature.

The way I frame it is: where is the pain that nobody else is positioned to solve well? When we started Lepton, the obvious temptation was to go up the stack and build applications ourselves, because that's where the visible value is. But I came out of years of building Caffe and then running infrastructure at Alibaba, and what I kept seeing was that the hard, unglamorous part of enterprise AI isn't the demo. It's making the thing run reliably, cheaply, and fast once real traffic hits it. Models change every few months, hardware is scarce and heterogeneous, and the gap between "works in a notebook" and "serves ten thousand concurrent users at a cost the CFO will sign off on" is enormous. That gap is infrastructure, and it's where we have a genuine, earned advantage.

So the first principle is: do what we're structurally good at and don't pretend to be a vertical expert in insurance claims or legal contracts. The people building those applications understand their customers far better than we ever will. Our job is to make them not have to think about GPUs, scheduling, quantization, batching, failover. If a customer has to hire three infra engineers just to run a model, we've failed.

The second principle is a bit more subtle, which is: look at what the big model providers and cloud vendors won't do, or will do badly. The frontier labs are optimizing for their own models. The hyperscalers sell you raw compute and happily let you waste it. There's a middle layer, model-agnostic, cost-obsessed, portable across clouds, that is genuinely underserved. Enterprises want optionality. They want to switch from one open model to another next quarter without rewriting everything, and they want to run on whatever hardware they can actually get. Being the neutral party there is a real position.

And the third thing is honestly just discipline about saying no. Every week a customer asks us to build some feature that's really an application concern, a RAG pipeline tuned for their documents, or an agent framework with their business logic baked in. It's tempting because they'll pay for it. But every one of those pulls us toward being a services company, and we lose the leverage that comes from solving a problem once and having it work for everyone. So the test I apply is: if we build this, does it make the platform better for the next hundred customers, or just for this one? If it's the latter, we help them find a partner or we expose the primitive so they can build it themselves.

I'll admit we don't always get it right. The boundary moves. Some things that felt like "application" two years ago, like evaluation tooling or prompt management, turned out to be common enough that they belong in the platform. So we revisit it. But the core bet hasn't changed: the application layer will be crowded and fast-moving, and the companies that make all of that run well underneath are going to matter for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses cloud vendors and infrastructure, but does not attribute a decision against building computing clusters to existing providers being adequate.

r002.rationale: It mentions RAG and model-agnostic infrastructure, but does not say that organizing customer data into an application pattern enables standardized model fine-tuning.

r003.rationale: It says application builders understand their customers far better and therefore Lepton should not act as a vertical expert.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is understanding what the customer actually needs to accomplish. An enterprise usually isn’t asking for a particular model or a particular piece of infrastructure. They’re trying to improve a workflow or build a product, and AI is one part of that.

Then we ask: Which problems are common across customers, and where can we contribute something meaningful? Those are the parts that make sense for us to take on. If every customer has to solve the same infrastructure problem before they can build their application, there’s an opportunity to solve it once and make it easier for everyone.

But the customer often understands their own business logic, data, and workflows much better than we do. We want to give them the tools to apply that knowledge. So the boundary comes down to where we can remove complexity while leaving customers enough flexibility to build what makes their application valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses taking on common infrastructure problems, but does not say the company avoids building computing clusters because cloud providers are adequate.

r002.rationale: It does not describe organizing customer data into an application pattern or enabling fine-tuning through a standardized service.

r003.rationale: It says customers understand their own business logic, data, and workflows much better, so the company leaves them flexibility to build what makes their application valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we start with the customer’s problem and work backward. Building an enterprise AI application involves a lot of pieces: your data, the model, the infrastructure, and the workflow around it. The question for us is where we can provide the most value and where there are already good solutions we can work with.

We don’t need to build every layer ourselves. If a customer already has a data platform they like, we should make it easy to connect to that. If there are good models available, we should help them use those models efficiently. Our job is to take away the complexity that doesn’t differentiate their business, so their team can focus on the application and the customer experience.

So the boundary is really driven by what customers need, what we’re good at, and what we can deliver reliably. We want to own enough of the problem to make the solution work, while being very deliberate about where we partner.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention computing clusters or say existing cloud infrastructure providers are adequate.

r002.rationale: It mentions connecting to customer data platforms, but not organizing data into an application pattern or enabling fine-tuning through a standardized service.

r003.rationale: It says decisions should reflect customer needs, but does not state that customers understand their business domains better or that vertical business decisions are left to them.
